Policies relating to the graduation of students from North Country Union High School with a diploma are based on standards required by the Vermont State Board of Education.
25 North Country credits are required for graduation.  Distribution of credits will involve:
4 years of English (4 credits)
3 years of social studies (3 credits) world history, government & economics & U.S. history
3 years of science (3 credits)
3 years of mathematics (3 credits)
3 semesters of physical education (1.5 credits)
1 semester of health education (.5 credits)
2 semester of fine arts (1 credit)
Elective courses (9 credits)
Students who fail a core course with at least a 2.0 or teacher recommendation are eligible to make up that course during the next semester or summer school immediately following the school year when the core course was failed.  A maximum of two courses may be taken during one complete summer school session.  The student may also repeat the course the following school year.
Freshmen and Juniors also participate in the State-wide assessment program (Cognia).

courses.description: This course is outdoor oriented with most days spent outside in all types of weather. Writing assignments take place atop the tallest mountains and looking out over the best vistas of the Northeast Kingdom. Reading assignments often take place in hardwood forests. This course runs in tandem with Adventure PE, a physically demanding outdoor PE course. The reading material provides the learner a level of insight into the mind and psyche of the world’s greatest explorers and adventurers that can only be gleaned by reading firsthand accounts and well-constructed retellings by the world’s greatest writers of nonfiction. Read about adventures to the world’s highest peaks, its frozen wastelands, its deserts, and its vast oceans. Read what kills even the most skilled and bravest adventurer. Read what it takes to survive. In addition to these texts, students read magazine articles published by the leaders in exploration written by the most skilled authors of our time. Students learn to record, journal, and construct written accounts of their own experiences and encounters gained during their enrollment in the Adventure PE Course – a high-level canoeing, kayaking, mountain biking, and backcountry skiing and snowboarding physical education course for juniors and seniors enrolled in either the Career Center or the High School.

courses.description: This course focuses on the genre of poetry and song lyrics. Students will read, listen to, analyze, discuss, and write about American poems and songs. Both songs and poetry are artistic expressions that reflect the diversity of American culture and Americans themselves. Common themes such as the American Dream and the conflict between the individual and the community are explored. Through a variety of important voices, this class ultimately asks students to reflect on their learning and discover for themselves what it means to be an American, how that perception may differ from those around them, and how understanding this can lead to unity and progress. Some commonly taught authors and artists include: Edgar Allan Poe, Taylor Swift, Walt Whitman, Emily Dickinson, Tupac Shakur, Langston Hughes, Maya Angelou, Robert Frost, and Katy Perry. Students will study poetic language, figurative language, and theme. The culminating project, a research presentation or paper, will be based on a chosen song or poem selected by each student.

courses.description: This course introduces students to the art and analysis of cinema through the close examination of movies from various decades and genres. Through observation and discussion, students will learn to “read” films by developing a critical eye for semiotics (the interpretation of signs and symbols), narrative construction, cinematography, and mise-en-scène (the setting of a scene). They will become active participants in the movie-watching experience by developing the skills to recognize, analyze, evaluate, and enjoy movies as a form of art and communication. This course is writing intensive. Students will examine various filming techniques and study the effective use of genre, character building, dialogue, plot, theme, motif, and symbolism. They will evaluate each movie on a 5-star scale and write blog-style reviews. They should also expect to write at least four academic papers using specific critical lenses and to craft several creative projects. **Parent/Guardian signature required if under 18. Film List: It’s Such a Beautiful Day, Casablanca , A Ghost Story, Parasite, Everything Everywhere All at Once, Arrival, The Grand Budapest Hotel, Fantastic Mr. Fox, Moonrise Kingdom, The Great Gatsby, Interstellar, Dunkirk, Aftersun, Napoleon Dynamite, Midnight in Paris, Arrival, One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest, True Grit, Knives Out , Bonnie and Clyde, The Maltese Falcon , and The Batman.

courses.course_name: Exploring the Northeast Kingdom: The Works of Howard Frank Mosher
courses.description: This course dives into the rich, evocative world of Howard Frank Mosher’s Where the Rivers Flow North and its accompanying short stories. Set in Vermont’s rugged Northeast Kingdom, Mosher’s works explore themes of resilience, cultural identity, environmental change, and the passage of time. Students will analyze the literary elements of Mosher’s stories, including his vivid use of setting, character development, and exploration of human connections to the natural world. Through close reading, creative projects, and analytical writing, students will gain a deep appreciation for Mosher’s storytelling and the way it reflects the spirit and struggles of rural New England life.

courses.course_name: Dystopian Literature and the End of the World
courses.description: Dystopian Literature and the End of the World plunges students into the gripping worlds of modern dystopian and apocalyptic masterpieces. Students will explore the haunting landscapes of The Road , a collapsing America in Parable of the Sower , post-pandemic chaos in Station 11 , and the politically charged dystopia of V for Vendetta . They will also read several short stories and poems from various authors and periods. This course is reading and discussion intensive. Students will read 40-50 pages between classes and engage in discussions that will challenge perceptions and ignite the imagination. They will dissect the complexities of these novels and short stories, unraveling hidden meanings, and connecting the dots to our present reality. There will be several analytical papers/projects and a formal research paper. The course final is to craft a short dystopian story.

courses.description: Elements of Horror in Literature focuses on the genre of horror and monster lore. Students will study the dark side of literature through an in-depth exploration of a variety of horror stories and novels. From classics such as Dracula and Macbeth to contemporary novels such as The Girl with All the Gifts , students will explore how the earliest gothic works are still influencing horror writers today. Students will also learn about the origins, lore, and creative imaginations that surround such things as zombies, vampires, ghosts, madness, death, and the things that go bump in the night. This course is reading and discussion intensive. Students will read 40-50 pages between classes and engage in discussions that will challenge perceptions and ignite the imagination. They will dissect the complexities of these novels and short stories, unraveling hidden meanings, and connecting the dots between modern fears and those of the past. There will be several analytical papers/projects and a formal research paper. The course final is to write and shoot a short horror film. **Several works will contain adult themes, including violence + disturbing images, mild language, and adrenaline-inducing terror .

courses.course_name: Our Stories: The Power of Memoir Writing
courses.description: In this engaging and thought-provoking English class, students will delve into the world of memoirs, a literary genre that blends personal reflection with storytelling. Through a variety of memoirs written by authors from diverse backgrounds, students will explore themes such as identity, memory, family, culture, and resilience. Throughout the semester, students will analyze different memoirs, examining the narrative techniques, voice, and structure used to convey the author’s personal journey. Discussions will focus on understanding the unique power of memoirs to reveal deeper truths about the human experience. Students will also engage in writing their own memoirs, reflecting on significant moments in their lives, and will learn how to craft compelling, authentic narratives. By the end of the course, students will gain a deeper appreciation for the art of memoir writing and an enhanced ability to connect personal experience with broader themes in literature.

courses.description: This course focuses on the vital and inspiring time period for African-Americans during the 1920’s. Through our studies, we will explore the genesis and meaning of this exciting period, attempting to come to a deeper understanding of the movement and why the legacies of the Harlem Renaissance continue to influence American literature and culture today.

Seven themes of equal importance – American and National Identity; Migration and Settlement; Politics and Power; Work, Exchange, and Technology; America in the World; Geography and the environment; and Culture and Society – provide areas of historical inquiry for investigation throughout the course. These require students to reason historically about continuity and change over time and make comparisons among various historical developments in different times and places. courses.description: Arts Integrated U.S. History Honors is the most challenging ACA Social Studies option for students. This course is strongly recommended for students considering Advanced Placement U.S. History or Advanced Placement European History in grade 12. Using a chronological framework, a thematic approach and an arts focus, this course begins with the growth of the United States from the American Civil War and Southern Reconstruction through to the conclusion of the Cold War. The course is designed to follow the major themes, ideas, politics and historical events in US history while making connections to its current realities in order to understand the effect history has had on our everyday life. Instruction will focus on American history, literature and fine arts related to the history curriculum as well as a review of writing, research, and basic study skills in addition to essays and research papers. Through the study of history through the lens of the arts from, and about, the historical periods and concepts that we are studying, we will make connections across these curricula to demonstrate how history is chronicled in the visual and performing arts of its time. This course will include additional writing and reading assignments outside of class. Writing assignments concentrate on essays of all types as well as the research paper.

courses.description: There are many ways to examine the history of the United States—in this course, we will put women at the center of the story. This course is a survey of the history of women in the United States from 1870 to the present. It examines the significant cultural, economic, and political developments that shaped the lives of American women, but places gender at the center of the historical analysis. The course also stresses the variety of women’s experiences, acknowledging the importance of race, ethnicity, and class in shaping female lives. We will discuss women’s political and social organizations, daily lives, economic roles, and the various ways in which gender roles have been constructed and received. The course traces a number of different interrelated themes from the late 18th century to the present: the changing conditions and ideas about unpaid housework and paid work; relations between different groups of women and the way relations of power have shaped these interactions; the ongoing political struggle to gain increased civil and political rights; and changing notions of "proper" roles for women. We will consider which ideas and assumptions within American culture have changed and which have stayed the same, and how these cultural factors have related to the material conditions through which people experience their daily lives. Finally, we will seek to understand who has gained and who has lost from these changes and continuities.
